'''Auktyon''' ({{langx|ru|АукцЫон}}, {{IPA|ru|ɐʊktsɨˈon|pron}}. Auktsyon) is a  [[Soviet]] and Russian [[Avantrock|avant-garde]] rock band from [[Saint Petersburg]].

The band was founded by {{ill|Leonid Fyodorov (musician)|lt=Leonid Fyodorov|ru|Фёдоров, Леонид Валентинович}} in 1978. Though they originally played [[post-punk]] and [[New wave music|new wave]], the group came to be influenced by European and Central Asian folk music, [[avant-garde jazz]], the poetry of Russian futurist [[Velimir Khlebnikov]], and aspects of Russian [[high culture]] and literature.

Auktyon was particularly popular from 1987 through 1995, but became less active in the late 1990s when Fyodorov began to produce records for [[Leningrad (band)|Leningrad]]. The group continues to play together and to release new albums. They toured the United States in 2006 in support of their first US release, the album ''Pioneer''. The group returned to the US in 2008 when they released the album ''Girls Sing.'' Between 2011 and 2020, Auktyon released several albums, while continuing to tour. The group also contributed to film projects, including the soundtrack for [[Aleksei Balabanov|Aleksei Balabanov's]] ''[[Me Too (2012 film)|Me Too]]'' (2012), and was featured in the 2014 documentary ''Eshche''. Their twelfth studio album, ''Sokrovishche'', was released in 2025.

== History ==

=== Early period ===

In the autumn of 1978, Leonid Fyodorov formed a band with his classmates. They started as a trio: Leonid Fyodorov (guitar), Dmitry Zaychenko (bass), and Alexey Vikhrev (drums). Two years later, two more of Fyodorov's school friends joined the group: Mikhail Makov (guitar, vocals) and Viktor Bondarik (bass), while Zaychenko switched to the organ. Around the same time, Sergey "Skvo" Skvortsov joined the group as a sound engineer and lighting technician.<ref name="Burlaka_2007">{{cite book |last=Burlaka |first=Andrey |title=Рок-энциклопедия: Популярная музыка в Ленинграде-Петербурге, 1965–2005 |trans-title=Rock Encyclopedia: Popular Music in Leningrad–Saint Petersburg, 1965–2005 |volume=1 |publisher=Амфора |year=2007 |isbn=978-5-367-00362-8 |language=ru}}</ref><ref name="Beumers_2005">{{cite book |last=Beumers |first=Birgit |title=Pop Culture Russia! |year=2005 |location=Santa Barbara |publisher=[[ABC-CLIO]] |isbn=1-85109-459-8}}</ref> The band began performing at dances in 1981, changing its name from Blue Boys to Paragraph and subsequently to Phaeton.<ref name="Margolis_2010">{{cite book |last=Margolis |first=Mikhail |title=АукцЫон: Книга учета жизни |trans-title=Auktyon: Book of Life |year=2010 |url=https://prochtenie.ru/fragments/15983 |publisher=Амфора |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241107095538/https://prochtenie.ru/fragments/15983 |archive-date=November 7, 2024 |access-date=November 6, 2026 |isbn=978-5-367-01615-4 |via=Прочтение}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Menshenina |first=Elena |date=13 March 2014 |title=Рокеры-романтики. Несколько фактов из истории «АукцЫона» |url=https://aif.ru/rm/rmfacts/1124044 |trans-title=Rock romantics: Some facts from the history of Auktyon |work=Аргументы и Факты |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140313230703/https://aif.ru/rm/rmfacts/1124044 |archive-date=March 13, 2014 |access-date=November 6, 2026}}</ref>

Around 1979, Oleg Garkusha became acquainted with Fyodorov. The group initially rehearsed in Fyodorov's apartment, where he composed the music using texts found in various books and magazines. Garkusha subsequently contributed his poetry to the band's repertoire. The group subsequently moved from Fyodorov's apartment to its first dedicated rehearsal space, the Leningradets youth club in Leningrad.<ref name="Margolis_2010" /><ref name="Spbdnevnik_2021">{{cite web |title=Олег Гаркуша: Перед вступлением в рок-клуб не спали всю ночь |url=https://special.spbdnevnik.ru/garkusha |trans-title=Oleg Garkusha: We stayed up all night before joining the rock club |website=Петербургский дневник |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210613163721/https://special.spbdnevnik.ru/garkusha |archive-date=June 13, 2021 |access-date=November 6, 2026}}</ref> At that time, the ensemble consisted of Alexey Vittel, Dmitry Zaychenko, Alexander Pompeyev (keyboards), Viktor Bondarik, and Mikhail Makov.<ref name="Margolis_2010" />

In 1980, Fyodorov met Dmitry Ozersky. Initially, Ozersky did not play any instruments and served solely as a lyricist. Following Fyodorov's advice, he began learning to play the keyboards—starting at a music school, though he later left the school and continued his studies independently.<ref name="Margolis_2010" /> 

By the spring of 1981, the lineup of Phaeton included: Leonid Fyodorov, Viktor Bondarik, Sergey Skvortsov, Dmitry Ozersky (keyboards), Sergey Melnik (guitar), and Yevgeny Chumichev (drums), as well as Oleg Garkusha—who, depending on the circumstances, served as a sound engineer, manager, and roadie, while also providing sound effects on stage.<ref name="Burlaka_2007" />

=== Joining the Leningrad Rock Club ===

In 1983, the band's bassist, Viktor Bondarik, began his military service and was replaced by Sergey Gubenko. Unsure of his own vocal abilities, Fyodorov invited Valery Nedomovny to serve as lead singer. Oleg Garkusha introduced the band—which was still called Phaeton at the time—to the group [[Aquarium (band)|Aquarium]]. Mikhail Feinstein, who was a member of Aquarium back then, advised them to join the newly founded [[Leningrad Rock Club]].<ref name="Burlaka_2007" />

On May 14, 1983, the band was admitted to the Rock Club as a candidate member and learned the date for their debut concert (scheduled for late autumn 1983). The lineup shifted: Nedomovny (vocals) and Melnik (guitar) left the band and were replaced by guitarist and singer Sergey Lobachev.<ref name="Burlaka_2007" /> In preparation for their first major performance, the band members chose a new name while browsing through a dictionary, but did not get beyond the letter "A"<ref>{{cite web |last=Курий |first=Сергей |date=November 9, 2016 |title=Происхождение названия группы АУКЦЫОН, ее символики и имиджа |url=https://www.kursivom.ru/происхождение-названия-аукцыон/ |trans-title=The Origin of the Band's Name AUKTSION, Its Symbolism, and Image |website=КУР.С.ИВ.ом |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261107073517/https://www.kursivom.ru/%D0%BF%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B8%D1%81%D1%85%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5-%D0%BD%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B2%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B8%D1%8F-%D0%B0%D1%83%D0%BA%D1%86%D1%8B%D0%BE%D0%BD/ |archive-date=November 7, 2026 |access-date=November 7, 2026}}</ref> before settling on "Auktyon".<ref name="Margolis_2010" /><ref name="OmskZdes_2023">{{cite web |date=July 6, 2023 |title=#МагияВинила: питерский "АукцЫон", или Дом на колёсах |url=https://omskzdes.ru/culture/82011.html |trans-title=#TheMagicOfVinyl: St. Petersburg's "Auktsyon", or A House on Wheels |website=Омск Здесь |language=ru |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250312134116/https://omskzdes.ru/culture/82011.html |archive-date=March 12, 2025 |access-date=November 7, 2026}}</ref>

The debut concert took place on November 18, 1983<ref name="Burlaka_2007" /> and, according to the band members, did not go particularly well. Following the concert, Lobachev, Gubenko, and Chumichev left the group.<ref name="Burlaka_2007" /><ref name="Margolis_2010" /><ref name="Angliya">{{cite interview |last=Garkusha |first=Oleg |interviewer-last=Mayorova |interviewer-first=Elena |title=Олег Гаркуша: «Успех — это дело случая» |url=https://angliya.com/publication/oleg-garkusha-uspeh-eto-delo-sluchaya/ |trans-title=Oleg Garkusha: "Success is a matter of chance" |publisher=Angliya |location=London |language=ru |date=October 25, 2018 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250522141634/https://angliya.com/publication/oleg-garkusha-uspeh-eto-delo-sluchaya/ |archive-date=May 22, 2025 |access-date=November 7, 2026}}</ref> The band experienced a series of other setbacks, including losing access to its rehearsal space and the theft of its equipment.<ref name="Angliya" /> Although the band had officially joined the Rock Club, a two-year period of inactivity followed (lasting until 1985). During this time, they were working on new material and about ten different drummers, guitarists, bassists, and singers passed through Auktyon, though none managed to establish a permanent place in the band.<ref name="OmskZdes_2023" /><ref name="Angliya" />

=== 1985–1986. Reunion and ''Come Back to Sorrento'' ===

By early 1985, following a hiatus, Auktyon resumed active rehearsals. The band's lineup stabilized: Bondarik (who had returned from military service) on bass, Ozersky on keyboards, Igor Cheridnik on drums, and Nikolai Fedorovich on alto saxophone. The band began working on a new program of songs. Fedorov, feeling insecure about his own singing, invited vocalist Sergey Rogozhin (whom Ozersky had "discovered") to join the band:

{{Quote box
 | quote      = <small>I walked into the Metallistov Palace of Culture and saw an empty hall with a panel of judges <…> It was absolute madness on stage: Garkusha was darting around with his bizarre, jerky movements, and Lenya Fedorov was singing—at the time, he couldn't seem to pronounce about 32 letters of the alphabet! <…> The judges watched for a while and finally delivered their verdict: 'Either take your lead singer to a speech therapist, or replace him, don't you think?' The members of Auktyon stood there, looking bewildered. They turned to the judges and declared, 'We do have a lead singer. He's right there—sitting in the audience.' Lenya was pointing at me—even though he had never seen or heard me before that moment! It was a complete gamble. And I didn't know a single Auktyon song! <…> As I walked toward the stage, I frantically wondered, 'What on earth am I going to sing?' Then, it hit me. Back in [[Zaporizhzhia]], where I grew up, a Hungarian band called Piramis had come to perform <…> There was one [[Power ballad|rock ballad]] of theirs that I had absolutely loved. That's the one I decided to perform. So, I began to sing it—[[a cappella]]—in Hungarian!… When I finished, a few scattered claps rang out behind me. It was the members of Auktyon themselves, applauding. Someone from the audience remarked: 'Well, it turns out you have an excellent lead singer—every word can be heard! Why didn't you mention him before?'</small>
 | source     = Sergey Rogozhin, ''Tabloid''<ref name="Tabloid_2014">{{cite magazine |date=July 12, 2014 |last=Sychev |first=Sergey |title=Radiola. God 1986 |url=http://tabloid.net.ru/radiola-god-1986/ |magazine=Tabloid |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210615120908/http://tabloid.net.ru/radiola-god-1986/ |archive-date=June 15, 2021 |access-date=November 7, 2026}}</ref>
 | width      = 100%
 | align      = right
 | bgcolor    = #f9f9f9
}}

Artist Kirill Miller also joined the group, taking charge of stage design and the musicians' visual style.<ref name="Margolis_2010" /> In May 1986, the band gave a successful performance at the 4th Leningrad Rock Festival with a lineup consisting of Leonid Fedorov (guitar, vocals), Oleg Garkusha (dancing, vocals), Sergey Rogozhin (vocals), Viktor Bondarik (bass), Dmitry Ozersky (keyboards, vocals), Nikolai Rubanov (saxophones, flutes), Nikolai Fedorovich (saxophone), and Igor Cheridnik (drums). Rogozhin received an award for best vocals, while Oleg Garkusha was recognized for his stage presence.<ref name="Auktyon.com_History_2001">{{cite web |title=History |url=http://www.auktyon.com/history.html |website=Auktyon.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010123132000/http://www.auktyon.com/history.html |archive-date=January 23, 2001 |access-date=November 7, 2026}}</ref> At the invitation of journalist and promoter Andrei Kolomoisky, the group also played two concerts at the ''Sever'' club in the city of [[Vyborg]].

Upon their return, the band began performing periodically at various community centers. One of these shows was recorded by Sergey Firsov and subsequently circulated as a [[cassette tape]] titled ''Rio-de-Shushary''. The recording is considered a rarity though in 2014, it was reissued on [[Compact disc|CD]] as part of the album ''{{ill|D'observer|ru|Д’обсервер}}''.

Fedorov, eager to capture their successful set on tape, led the group through various recording sessions to produce the album ''{{ill|Vernis v Sorrento|ru|Вернись в Сорренто (альбом)}}'' (''Return to Sorrento''), which was not officially released until several years later.<ref name="Margolis_2010" />

=== 1987: A New Program and Lineup Changes ===

By 1987, Auktyon had already become a popular band. They made a cameo appearance in the film ''{{ill|The Burglar (1987 film)|lt=The Burglar|ru|Взломщик (фильм, 1987)}}'', with Oleg Garkusha playing a supporting role as a friend of the protagonist.

Fedorov and Ozersky prepared a new set of songs titled ''Everything Is Calm in Baghdad'' (''{{ill|V Bagdade vse spokoyno|ru|В Багдаде всё спокойно (альбом)}}''). Meanwhile, saxophonist Nikolai Fedorovich left the band. According to Ozersky, the material was inspired by the works of [[E.T.A. Hoffmann]], envisioned as a kind of magical land: "We imagined this 'dreamland' as something like the United Arab Emirates—perhaps one where the oil had run out, or something similar. In essence, these were purely speculative attempts to transpose Hoffmann's world into our own contemporary reality."

The program was unveiled in June 1987 at the 5th Leningrad Rock Festival. During the performance, the band incorporated Eastern-inspired motifs into their stage design and costumes. The new songs, however, received a lukewarm response from both the audience and critics. To make matters worse, Rogozhin—the vocalist for whom the program had been specifically tailored—announced his departure from Auktyon to join the band {{ill|Forum (band)|lt=Forum|ru|Форум (группа)}}. Guitarist Igor Skaldin joined briefly, followed by Dmitry Matkovsky, and the lineup was further bolstered by the addition of percussionist Pavel Litvinov. Dancer {{ill|Vladimir Vesyolkin|ru|Весёлкин, Владимир Олегович}} also joined the group. Ultimately, the band set aside the "Everything Is Calm in Baghdad" program and began working on new material.<ref name="Burlaka_2007" />

=== 1988: ''How I Became a Traitor'' ===

Following an active touring schedule in 1987, violinist and vocalist {{ill|Yevgeny Dyatlov|ru|Дятлов, Евгений Валерьевич}} joined the band. In May 1988, the group began recording the album ''How I Became a Traitor'' (''{{ill|Kak ya stal predatelem|ru|Как я стал предателем}}''), marking their first experience working in a professional studio environment. The album's title was taken from a line in a poem by Oleg Garkusha, "That's How I Became a Traitor"—a phrase inspired by a television program about a former [[TASS]] employee who had become a spy. This line was later incorporated into the lyrics of the song "New Year's Song" ("Novogodnyaya pesnya"), which appears on the album. For reasons unknown, Kirill Miller, who designed the album artwork, rendered the title as ''How I Became a Traitor'' (''Kak ya stal predatelem'').<ref name="Kushnir_1999">{{cite book |last=Semelyak |first=Max |chapter=Аукцыон — Как я стал предателем |trans-chapter=Auktyon — How I Became a Traitor |title=100 Magnitoalbomov Sovetskogo Roka |trans-title=100 Cassette Albums of Soviet Rock |editor-last=Kushnir |editor-first=Alexander |year=1999 |pages=144-145 |url=http://www.rockanet.ru/100/89.phtml |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110831110138/http://www.rockanet.ru/100/89.phtml |archive-date=August 31, 2011 |via=RockaNet.ru |language=ru}}</ref> "We moved away from songs that came, so to speak, from the 'head'—from a purely intellectual approach—toward somewhat more metaphysical material, attempting to push beyond the boundaries we had set for ourselves. While working on this material, I felt a sense of personal growth; I realized I was maturing and beginning to think differently than I had before", noted Dmitry Ozersky. On June 5, 1988, the band presented this material at the 6th Leningrad Rock Festival. In his diary, Vladimir Veselkin described the concert: "It was a triumph for the band. Everything was being filmed."<ref>{{cite web |last=Veselkin |first=Vladimir |title=Дневник. 1988 год |url=https://www.auctyon.ru/article/dnev88.html |trans-title=Diary. 1988 |website=Auktyon.ru |language=ru |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927042748/http://www.auctyon.ru/article/dnev88.html |archive-date=September 27, 2011 |access-date=April 21, 2011}}</ref> Dissatisfied with what he perceived as a secondary role within the group, Dyatlov announced his departure.

Throughout the summer and autumn of 1988, the band toured extensively across the [[USSR]]. Meanwhile, drummer Igor Cheridnik left to join the band {{ill|Igry|ru|Игры (группа)}}, prompting an urgent search for a replacement. After considering several other candidates, the position was filled by Boris Shaveynikov, who joined the band just before their tour of the [[Russian Far East|Far East]]. It is to Boris that the band owes its name; he wrote it with a [[Eye dialect|deliberate misspelling]]—"AuktsYon" (АукцЫон). The band liked the name, and it stuck. At the end of 1988, the group took part in a memorial concert for [[Alexander Bashlachev]] at the [[Luzhniki Sports Palace]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Smirnov |first=Ilya |title=Мемориал Александра Башлачёва в Лужниках, 20.11.1988 |trans-title=Alexander Bashlachev Memorial in Luzhniki, November 20, 1988 |magazine=[[:ru:Сельская молодёжь|Сельская молодёжь]] |issue=11 |page=38 |date=1989 |language=ru |via=Narod.ru |url=https://gruppakino.narod.ru/mitn.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070304011833/https://gruppakino.narod.ru/mitn.html |archive-date=March 4, 2007 |access-date=November 10, 2026}}</ref>

Late that year, the December issue of ''{{ill|Aurora (Russian magazine)|lt=Aurora|ru|Аврора (журнал, Санкт-Петербург)}}'' magazine published a list of the best Soviet rock albums, compiled over the previous six months based on the opinions of critics and readers. Not a single Auktyon record appeared on the 25-album list. Nevertheless, the band's recordings found a certain level of success in the West, and in 1989, the group embarked on its first tour abroad.<ref>{{cite web |last=Boyarinov |first=Denis |date=October 16, 2015 |title=Tantsor riska |url=https://takiedela.ru/2015/10/veselkin/ |trans-title=Dancer of Risk |website=Takiye Dela |language=ru |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250312104941/https://takiedela.ru/2015/10/veselkin/ |archive-date=March 12, 2025 |access-date=March 12, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Khomyakova |first=Natasha |date=January 31, 2022 |title=Artefakty shou-biznesa 1980-kh na vystavke «Viktor Tsoy. Put' geroya» |url=https://i-m-i.ru/post/tsoi-exhibition |trans-title=Show Business Artifacts of the 1980s at the Exhibition "Viktor Tsoi: The Hero's Journey" |work=[[:ru:Институт музыкальных инициатив|IMI Journal]] |publisher=Institute of Music Initiatives (IMI) |language=ru |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250312111214/https://i-m-i.ru/post/tsoi-exhibition |archive-date=March 12, 2025 |access-date=March 12, 2025}}</ref>

=== 1989: Tours Abroad ===

On February 1, 1989, Auktyon arrived in Berlin, accompanied by the bands [[Zvuki Mu]] and [[Va-Bank]], as well as singer Ekaterina Surzhikova. Two months later, the band toured France alongside [[Kino (band)|Kino]] and Zvuki Mu to promote the CD ''How I Became a Traitor'' (''Kak ya stal predatelem''), which had been released there. It was also in France that the band had a momentous encounter with [[Alexei Khvostenko]]—a figure who would later play a significant role in both the band's own work and the solo projects of Leonid Fyodorov. These trips to France were also linked to a well-known scandal involving the band. During a festival in [[Le Bourget]], Vladimir Veselkin performed a mock striptease while the song "Nepman" was playing, ending up in nothing but flesh-colored undergarments. This incident drew negative coverage in the Soviet newspapers ''[[Sovetskaya Kultura]]'' and ''[[Komsomolskaya Pravda]]''. ''Komsomolskaya Pravda'' published an article titled "Pop Music? Showing off real skill proved difficult—so they showed off bad taste instead", accusing the band of vulgarity and poor taste.<ref>{{cite news |last=Dolgopolov |first=Nikolai |date=April 12, 1989 |title=ЗВУКИ МУ, КИНО, АУКЦЫОН |url=http://www.nneformat.ru/archive/?id=4208 |trans-title=Sounds of Mu, Kino, Auktyon |newspaper=[[Komsomolskaya Pravda]] |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121022164251/http://www.nneformat.ru/archive/?id=4208 |archive-date=October 22, 2012 |access-date=November 8, 2026 |via=Наш НеФормат}}</ref> Vladimir Veselkin gathered signatures from prominent figures in the Leningrad cultural scene and succeeded in getting an "Open Letter from the Band Auktyon" published in the May 12, 1989, issue of ''Sovetskaya Kultura''.<ref name="Margolis_2010" /> ''Komsomolskaya Pravda'' offered no response. Later, Veselkin repeated the act during the television program ''{{ill|Musical Ring|ru|Музыкальный ринг}}''. The performance was poorly received, prompting a comment from the audience: "Your deliberately degenerate performance style serves to discredit Soviet rock".<ref name="Margolis_2010" /><ref>{{cite interview |last=Veselkin |first=Vladimir |interviewer= |url=http://www.bostontea.narod.ru/veselkin.html |title=Interview |work=Boston Tea Party |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521183539/http://www.bostontea.narod.ru/veselkin.html |archive-date=May 21, 2013 |access-date=November 8, 2026 |via=Narod.ru}}</ref> That summer, the band recorded the album ''Everything Is Calm in Baghdad'' at the Leningrad Recording Studio. On the night of June 11–12, 1989, Auktyon closed out the final (seventh) Leningrad Rock Festival. During rehearsals that year, the band was already actively playing the tracks "Airplane", "Pioneer", "Love", and "Tattletale"—songs that would soon make up their next album.

=== 1990–1991: ''Zhopa'' and ''Bodun'' ===

By 1990, the band was actively working on new material. A friendship developed between bassist Viktor Bondarik and drummer Boris Shaveynikov, which helped strengthen the band's rhythm section. Fyodorov arranged for recording sessions at [[Stas Namin]]'s studio, where the album ''[[Zhopa]]'' (''Ass'') was recorded during the winter. The vinyl release featured a truncated version of the album, and for censorship reasons, the title was changed to ''Duplo'' ("Hollow/Cavity"). Also in 1990, the record ''V Bagdade vsyo spokoyno'' (''All Is Quiet in Baghdad'')—recorded back in 1989—was released by the Melodiya label. In May and June, the band took part in the ''Rock of Clean Water'' (''Rok chistoy vody'') festival.

In 1991, the band recorded the album ''{{ill|Bodun|ru|Бодун}}'' (''Hangover''). Its cover art was the last one designed by Miller. The song "Stolby" ("Pillars") was omitted from the initial release due to profanity in the lyrics. These new albums differed significantly in style from the band's previous work—partly due to the influence of Shaveynikov, whose drumming was "heavier." The material became darker and more [[Musical improvisation|improvisational]]. The band toured extensively in Germany, with the tours organized by a German named Christoph Karsten. Miller and Vesyolkin began to drift away from the band; the group itself had grown weary of Vesyolkin's behavior on stage, as he was prone to heavy alcohol abuse. Oleg Garkusha, who was also struggling with heavy alcohol abuse, began to play an increasingly minor role in the band. In 1992, Vesyolkin left the group to pursue a solo project.

=== Mid-1990s. ''Chainik vina'' (''A Teapot of Wine'') and ''Ptitsa'' (''Bird'') ===

Fedorov had long harbored the idea of ​​recording songs by his friend Alexei Khvostenko. However, Khvostenko lived in France—a country where Auktyon had little time to spare during their tours. In 1992, having finally secured the necessary paperwork, Khvostenko arrived in Russia aboard a plane carrying humanitarian aid. Working at the Titanic studio, the band—joined by Khvostenko—recorded the album ''{{ill|Chainik vina|ru|Чайник вина}}'' in a rather short timeframe. Fedorov would later describe it as one of Auktyon's finest works. During this period, Auktyon began touring Europe more frequently, even purchasing a used bus for the purpose.<ref name="Margolis_2010" />

In 1993, the band began recording the album ''{{ill|Ptitsa (album)|lt=Ptitsa|ru|Птица (альбом)}}'' (''Bird''), which would go on to become one of their most popular releases. This was largely due to the inclusion of the song "[[The Road (Auktyon song)|The Road]]" on the soundtrack for Alexei Balabanov's highly successful film ''[[Brother 2]]'' (''Brat-2''), released in 2000. The recording process, including rehearsals, took about six months. The title track was composed by Fedorov and Garkusha while they were staying in the countryside during the attempted coup. Relations within the band were strained at the time; according to Fedorov, the group was on the verge of breaking up.<ref>{{cite web |last=Курий |first=Сергей |title="The Птица" (1993) |url=http://www.ytime.com.ua/ru/50/2059 |website=Рок-толкование |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141023022508/http://www.ytime.com.ua/ru/50/2059 |archive-date=October 23, 2014 |access-date=April 21, 2011}}</ref> Nevertheless, the other band members were pleased with the album. While Fedorov considers the individual songs on the record to be among the best he and Ozersky ever wrote, he generally views ''Ptitsa'' as one of the band's failures.

It suddenly dawned on me that you could create amazing things using minimal resources, without having to come up with anything particularly elaborate. ''Ptitsa'' [Bird] was an attempt to record something like that—without Khvost, just with Auktyon. But the attempt failed. We couldn't manage to make a simple record; the arrangements ruined ''Ptitsa''. Our previous albums—''Kak ya stal predatelem'' [How I Became a Traitor], ''Bodun'', and ''Zhopa'' [Ass]—were recorded exactly the way we wanted them to be; they are far more coherent than ''Ptitsa''.
 | source     = Leonid Fyodorov, Margolis (2010)<ref name="Margolis_2010" />
 | width      = 100%

The album was released in two editions, six months apart (a German version and a Russian version).

=== The Second Half of the 1990s ===

[[File:Chlebnikow.jpg|thumb|Auktyon explored the poetry of [[Velimir Khlebnikov]] in collaboration with avant-garde poet [[Alexei Khvostenko]]. Their 1995 album ''Zhilets vershin'' (''Dweller of the Peaks'') combines Khlebnikov's poems, selected and adapted by Khvostenko, with music by the band, creating a new interpretation of the poet's work.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Vatueva |first=Viktoria A. |title=Poetry of Velimir Khlebnikov in the Works of the Band "Auktyon": On the Example of the Album "Zhilets Vershin" |journal=RSUH/RGGU Bulletin. Literary Theory. Linguistics. Cultural Studies |issue=8 |year=2021 |pages=75–85 |doi=10.28995/2686-7249-2021-8-75-85}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Volkov |first=Alexander V. |date=December 22, 2016 |title=Auktyon: Zhilets vershin (1995/2016) |journal=[[InRock]] |issue=77}}</ref>]]

Following the album ''Ptitsa'', the band entered a creative crisis. Fyodorov managed to overcome this after being introduced to the poetry of Velimir Khlebnikov (with the help of Khvostenko). In 1995, the band—together with Khvostenko—recorded an album based on Khlebnikov's poems, titled ''Zhilets vershin'' (''Dweller of the Peaks'').

The band's activity within Russia began to decline, though Auktyon continued to tour Europe (with particularly frequent performances in Germany).<ref name="Burlaka_2007" /> In November 1995, guitarist Dmitry Matkovsky was dismissed from the group. According to Ozersky, the conflict stemmed from both musical differences—Matkovsky favored a more disciplined approach to performance, while saxophonist Rubanov advocated for improvisation—and personal friction. Matkovsky was replaced by tuba player Mikhail Kolovsky. On July 22, 1996, Oleg Garkusha traveled to America to undergo treatment for alcoholism; he stopped drinking thereafter.

In 1997, the albums ''Vernis v Sorrento'' (''Return to Sorrento'') and ''D'observer'' (a recording of a 1986 concert at the [[Pulkovo Observatory]]) were officially released for the first time. That same year, Fyodorov released his debut solo album, the acoustic ''Chetyrespolovinoytonny'' (''Four and a Half Tons'').

Throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s, Leonid Fyodorov focused on solo projects, collaborating with various other musicians, and producing albums for [[Leningrad (band)|Leningrad]].<ref name="Beumers_2005" /> In 1999, the band released two singles: ''{{ill|Zimy ne budet|ru|Зимы не будет (альбом)}}'' (''There Won't Be a Winter''), credited to "Auktyon, Volkov, Kurashov," and ''Nebo napopolam'' (''Sky Split in Half''), a collaboration between the band and [[Leonid Soybelman]].

=== From 2000 to the Present ===

In 2002, the album ''{{ill|Eto Mama|ru|Это мама}}'' (''This Is Mom'') was released—a recording of the band's live set—featuring two new songs, "Yakorya" ("Anchors") and "O Pogode" ("About the Weather"), as well as "Zaveduyushchiy (Koporye)" ("The Manager (Koporye)"), which had previously appeared on Fyodorov's 1997 solo album.<ref>{{cite web |title=«Это мама» |url=https://www.leonidfedorov.ru/emama.htm |website=Leonid Fyodorov official website |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030305192816/https://www.leonidfedorov.ru/emama.htm |archive-date=March 5, 2003 |access-date=November 8, 2026}}</ref> On December 15, 2005, percussionist Pavel Litvinov passed away following a second stroke.

Auktyon toured the United States in 2006<ref name="BostonGlobe_2006">{{cite news |last=Mitter |first=Siddhartha |date=24 March 2006 |title=By way of Russia, art-rock for art's sake |newspaper=[[Boston Globe]] |page=D.1}}</ref><ref name="NYTimes_2005">{{cite news |last=Sisario |first=Ben |date=November 21, 2005 |title=Arts, Briefly |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/11/21/arts/arts-briefly.html |url-access=subscription |newspaper=[[New York Times]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150529191203/https://www.nytimes.com/2005/11/21/arts/arts-briefly.html |archive-date=May 29, 2015 |access-date=November 8, 2026}}</ref> in support of their first US release, the compilation album ''[[Pioneer (Auktyon album)|Pioneer]]''. The next full-length studio album, ''{{ill|Devushki Poyut|ru|Девушки поют}}'' (''Girls Are Singing''), was released in 2007, following a 12-year hiatus.<ref name="NYTimes_2008">{{cite news |last=Sisario |first=Ben |date=24 March 2006 |title=Pop and Rock Listings |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/03/21/arts/music/21pop.html |url-access=subscription |newspaper=[[New York Times]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180106024653/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/03/21/arts/music/21pop.html |archive-date=January 6, 2018 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref> It was recorded in New York at Stratosphere Sound Studios, with contributions from American musicians [[Marc Ribot]], [[John Medeski]], [[Frank London]], and [[Ned Rothenberg]], alongside Russian double bassist Vladimir Volkov.<ref>{{cite magazine |date=October 2006 |title=Рецензия на концерт |trans-title=Concert review |magazine=[[:ru:Fuzz (журнал)|FUZZ]] |volume=10 |issue=157 |language=ru}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=«Девушки поют» |url=https://www.leonidfedorov.ru/dp.htm |trans-title=Girls Sing |website=Leonid Fyodorov official website |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250518071621/http://www.leonidfedorov.ru/dp.htm |archive-date=May 18, 2025 |access-date=November 8, 2026}}</ref> In 2008 and 2009,  they toured the US again in support of the album.<ref name="NYTimes_2008" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Vigil |first=Delfin |date=27 March 2008 |title=Auktyon. Eclectic band formed in the former Soviet Union and, 20 years later, strange, loud rock plays a key role in the group's musical stylings |newspaper=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] |page=G.4}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=18 March 2008 |last=Drozdowski |first=Ted |title=Auktyon - CD Reviews |url=http://thephoenix.com/Boston/music/58205-auktyon-girls-sing/ |newspaper=[[The Phoenix (newspaper)|The Phoenix]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121014185438/http://thephoenix.com/Boston/music/58205-auktyon-girls-sing/ |archive-date=2012-10-14 |access-date=2012-09-19}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Horowitz |first=Steve |date=31 March 2008 |title=Auktyon: Girls Sing |url=https://www.popmatters.com/auktyon-girls-sing-2496176373.html |work=[[PopMatters]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190805154107/https://www.popmatters.com/auktyon-girls-sing-2496176373.html |archive-date=August 5, 2019 |access-date=November 7, 2026}}</ref> 

On October 7, 2011, the band unveiled a new album, ''{{ill|Yula (album)|lt=Yula|ru|Юла (альбом)}}'' (''Spinning Top''), which was recorded without the involvement of foreign guest musicians. The album was produced on a tight schedule—over the course of just 11 days—at the Parametrika studio in Moscow. Vladimir Volkov, who had collaborated with Fyodorov on his solo projects and performed live with Auktyon for several years, took part in the recording.<ref>{{cite web |title=«Аукцыон»: так решил волчок |url=https://rollingstone.ru/articles/Auktsion:-tak-reshil-volchok |trans-title="Auktyon": The Spinning Top Decided So |website=[[Rolling Stone|Rolling Stone Russia]] |language=ru |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111105060215/http://rollingstone.ru/articles/Auktsion:-tak-reshil-volchok |archive-date=November 5, 2011 |access-date=October 8, 2011}}</ref> The album's release was preceded by the launch of the band's official YouTube channel on September 21 of that same year. Trumpeter [[Yuriy Parfyonov]] also participated in the recording; he performed with the band during the album's launch concerts and subsequently became a permanent member of the group. In 2012, the final film by Russian director Aleksei Balabanov, ''[[Me Too (2012 film)|Me Too]]'', was released. Oleg Garkusha played the lead role of "The Musician", Leonid Fyodorov served as the film's composer, and the soundtrack consists entirely of songs by the band and Fyodorov himself.<ref>{{cite news |last=Зинцов |first=Олег |date=December 12, 2012 |title=«Я тоже хочу» Алексея Балабанова: Счастливый конец стал сюжетом |url=https://www.vedomosti.ru/lifestyle/articles/2012/12/12/k_schastyu |trans-title=Alexey Balabanov's ''Me Too'': A Happy Ending Became the Story |newspaper=[[Vedomosti]] |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702081022/https://www.vedomosti.ru/lifestyle/articles/2012/12/12/k_schastyu |archive-date=2 July 2023 |access-date=2 July 2023}}</ref>

In 2013, the band celebrated its 30th anniversary with a series of concerts in cities including Moscow, Saint Petersburg, [[Smolensk]], [[Kyiv]], and [[Dnipropetrovsk]]. In December, to mark the 20th anniversary of their album ''Ptitsa'', the group held two exclusive concerts in Moscow and Saint Petersburg, during which they performed every track from that album.

2014 saw the release of the documentary film ''Eshche'' (''More''), directed by [[Dmitry Lavrinenko]]. Filmed over the course of seven years, the project followed the band on tour; the director was present in the studio during the creation of the album ''Yula'', handed the camera to the musicians themselves when they traveled to America to record with Medeski and Ribot, and captured the most intimate moments of the band's performances.

Preview screenings of the film took place in Moscow and Saint Petersburg during the summer. In September 2014, a "film marathon" began, with screenings held in more than 15 cities across Russia and beyond. In several locations—including Moscow, [[Yekaterinburg]], [[Kaluga]], and [[Minsk]]—the band's concerts were timed to coincide with the release of the film. According to director Lavrinenko, a second film is expected to be released soon, focusing on the solo work of Leonid Fedorov and his musical projects with Volkov, [[Sergey Starostin]], and others.

On December 4, 2014—coinciding with the birthday of A. Khvostenko—a posthumous album titled ''Scorpion'' was released, featuring contributions from musicians of the band Auktyon. The album contains 22 tracks in which the author performs his own poetry, as well as fables written in collaboration with [[Anri Volokhonsky]]. The musical arrangements for these poems were created by A. Gerasimov and the members of the band themselves.

Due to various circumstances, work on ''Scorpion'' spanned nearly a decade—from 2004 to 2013—during which time both key figures of the project, Khvostenko and Gerasimov, passed away. Following Khvostenko's death, his daughter, Anna, stepped in to serve as a "critic and advisor" to the musicians during the recording process. The album's title was suggested by Auktyon double bassist Vladimir Volkov, inspired by the poem "Under the Sign of the Scorpion" ("Pod znakom Skorpiona"), which is included in the collection. Much of the recording took place at the apartment of the band's frontman, Leonid Fedorov—who acted as the album's de facto producer—and he subsequently mixed all the tracks in his home studio.

== Artistry ==

=== Musical style ===

Contemporary descriptions have associated it with art rock, post-punk, free jazz, [[Latin percussion]] and the sound of military [[marching bands]].<ref name="TorontoStar_2006" /> A 2005 ''[[Willamette Week]]'' article described Auktyon's approach as a form of genre-splicing, identifying influences from Russian folk music, [[avant-jazz]], [[jazz fusion]], and [[psychedelic music]] of the 1960s.<ref name="WillametteWeek_2005">{{cite news |last=Dundas |first=Zach |date=April 26, 2005 |title=Glasnost for Others |url=https://www.wweek.com/portland/article-4348-glasnost-for-others.html |newspaper=[[Willamette Week]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261109025030/https://www.wweek.com/portland/article-4348-glasnost-for-others.html |archive-date=November 9, 2026 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref> A 2008 review in ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'' further identified psychedelic grooves, 1980s pop and contemporary [[World music|ethnic fusion]], particularly Slavic folk music and ska, in the band's sound.<ref name="Inquirer_2008">{{cite news |last=Adler |first=David R. |date=24 March 2008 |title=Auktyon creates own style, aura |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/entertainment/20080324_Auktyon_creates_own_style__aura.html |url-access=subscription |newspaper=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261031005246/https://www.inquirer.com/philly/entertainment/20080324_Auktyon_creates_own_style__aura.html |archive-date=October 31, 2026 |access-date=November 8, 2026}}</ref>

The ''[[Boston Globe]]'' noted the prominence of low-register horns and described connections between ska and [[klezmer]] in the band's music.<ref name="BostonGlobe_2006" /> A 1995 review, the German newspaper ''[[die tageszeitung|taz]]'' described the music on the album ''Ptiza'' as a combination of Russian folk harmonies, klezmer rhythms and jazz, with predominantly acoustic instrumentation.<ref name="taz_1995">{{cite news |last=Rademacher |first=Noël |date=October 6, 1995 |title=Hoffnungsvoll hysterisch |url=https://taz.de/Hoffnungsvoll-hysterisch/\!1490038/ |newspaper=[[die tageszeitung]] |language=de |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261109032008/https://taz.de/Hoffnungsvoll-hysterisch/!1490038/ |archive-date=November 9, 2026 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref> Reviewing ''Girls Sing'' in 2008, the ''[[Boston Phoenix]]'' highlighted the album's range from noise-influenced [[cool jazz]] to acoustic [[Romani music#Romani folk music|Gypsy folk]].<ref name="BostonPhoenix_2008">{{cite news |last=Drozdowski |first=Ted |date=March 18, 2008 |title=Auktyon |url=https://thephoenix.com/Boston/music/58205-auktyon-girls-sing/ |newspaper=[[The Boston Phoenix]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080928212234/https://thephoenix.com/Boston/music/58205-auktyon-girls-sing/ |archive-date=September 28, 2008 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref>

The band's musical identity is also associated with theatrical performance. A 1989 ''[[die tageszeitung|taz]]'' concert review described Auktyon's mixture of jazz, new wave, punk, Russian folk music, modern dance and theatre, while noting the group's costumes and stage antics.<ref name="taz_1989">{{cite news |last=Höfer |first=Petra |date=February 9, 1989 |title=Im siebten blockfreien Pophimmel |url=https://taz.de/Im-siebten-blockfreien-Pophimmel/\!1822941/ |newspaper=[[die tageszeitung]] |language=de |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261109032745/https://taz.de/Im-siebten-blockfreien-Pophimmel/!1822941/ |archive-date=November 9, 2026 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref> ''[[Willamette Week]]'' likewise characterized the group by its absurdist stage show and musical intensity, while describing its compositions as unconventional, genre-crossing pieces rather than conventional verse-and-chorus songs.<ref name="WillametteWeek_2005" />

=== Influences ===

Auktyon's musical influences encompassed a wide range of genres, including new wave, post-punk, hard rock, art rock, [[free jazz]] and contemporary classical music. In a 2013 interview with ''[[Colta.ru|Colta]]'', saxophonist Nikolai Rubanov recalled that [[the Cure]] and [[the Police]] had a particularly strong influence on the band during its early years. He also cited free jazz, [[Led Zeppelin]], art rock and contemporary [[chamber music]] among his own musical interests.<ref name="colta_2013">{{cite web |last=Kashapov |first=Radif |date=October 4, 2013 |title=У нас ведь еще и анархия |url=https://www.colta.ru/articles/music_modern/687-u-nas-ved-esche-i-anarhiya |trans-title=There's also anarchy among us |website=[[Colta.ru]] |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210514112751/https://www.colta.ru/articles/music_modern/687-u-nas-ved-esche-i-anarhiya |archive-date=May 14, 2021 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref>

In a 1989 interview with ''[[Die Tageszeitung|taz]]'', guitarist Leonid Fyodorov named the Cure among his favourite bands, while guitarist Dmitry Matkovsky cited [[Talking Heads]]. The interview also noted that the band's members had diverse musical tastes, including Arabic music and hard rock.<ref name="taz_1989" />

In a 1995 interview, Fyodorov identified [[the Beatles]] as his most significant musical influence, describing their impact on rock music as particularly transformative.<ref name="rockarchive_1995">{{cite web |date=1995 |title=АУКЦЫОН: Делать рок-н-ролл слишком просто |url=https://www.rockarchive.ru/text/n-1/265/index.shtml |trans-title=Auktyon: Making rock 'n' roll is too easy |website=Rockarchive.ru |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081023202133/https://www.rockarchive.ru/text/n-1/265/index.shtml |archive-date=October 23, 2008 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref>

In a 2024 interview, vocalist Oleg Garkusha recalled that the band's early musical environment was strongly influenced by British new wave, mentioning Talking Heads, The Police, [[The Clash]], [[Bryan Ferry]], [[Bad Manners]], and [[Madness (band)|Madness]]. He also noted similarities between the early music of Auktyon and the Police.<ref name="snob_2024">{{cite web |last=Spesivtsev |first=Egor |date=May 28, 2024 |title=«У меня нет ни слуха, ни голоса, ничего». Фронтмен «АукцЫона» Олег Гаркуша о любимых пластинках, сольном творчестве и концерте в тюрьме |url=https://snob.ru/music/u-menia-net-ni-slukha-ni-golosa-nichego-frontmen-auktsyona-oleg-garkusha-o-liubimykh-plastinkakh-solnom-tvorchestve-i-kontserte-v-tiurme/ |trans-title=I have neither an ear nor a voice, nothing: Auktyon's frontman Oleg Garkusha on favourite records, solo work and a prison concert |website=[[:ru:Сноб (медиапроект)|Snob]] |language=ru |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240620175706/https://snob.ru/music/u-menia-net-ni-slukha-ni-golosa-nichego-frontmen-auktsyona-oleg-garkusha-o-liubimykh-plastinkakh-solnom-tvorchestve-i-kontserte-v-tiurme/ |archive-date=June 20, 2024 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref>

'''Martin Evans''' (1916 – 29 December 2003) was influential in the field of model engineering and locomotive design, and also worked as the technical editor and eventually managing editor of the English magazine ''[[Model Engineer magazine|Model Engineer]]''.<ref name="Index 2018">{{cite web | title=Martin Evans | website=Index | date=2018-05-15 | url=https://modelengineeringwebsite.com/Martin_Evans.html | access-date=2022-07-09}}</ref> His editorship, along with other changes in staff, helped keep the magazine on track after experiencing some decline following the death of locomotive designer [[Curly Lawrence]].<ref>Model Engineer, nr. 4218, 5 March 2004, p.250</ref> Evans inaugurated the International Model Locomotive Efficiency Competition (IMLEC) in 1969.<ref name="auto">Model Engineer nr. 4213, 23 January 2004, p.73.</ref> An erudite editor, Evans worked with a pool of other knowledgeable contributors during a time considered to be the height of British toolroom engineering. Evans retired from the magazine in June 1977, continuing his concentration on locomotive design. He died December 29, 2003.<ref name="auto"/> 
==Locomotive designs==
Many model locomotive designs in a range of gauges were serialised by Martin Evans in the pages of Model Engineer. Some of the castings used to machine and build these designs are still available from a few commercial suppliers as are some of the laser cut components.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ajreeves.com|title=AJ Reeves - ajreeves.com|website=Ajreeves.com|accessdate=3 October 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.blackgates.co.uk/|title=Home Page|website=Blackgates.co.uk|accessdate=3 October 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.modelengineerslaser.co.uk|title=Model Engineers Laser|website=Modelengineerslaser.co.uk|accessdate=3 October 2017}}</ref> Some of the earlier designs along with discussion threads among engineers of locomotive models can be seen in various web forums on the internet.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://freespace.virgin.net/simplex.steam/index.htm |title=The Simplex web site |accessdate=2011-02-05 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110415054112/http://freespace.virgin.net/simplex.steam/index.htm |archivedate=2011-04-15 }} </ref> They are frequently seen both on model railway society tracks and second-hand markets.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stationroadsteam.com/ |title=Station Road Steam - live steam models |accessdate=2010-03-15 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100327190936/http://www.stationroadsteam.com/ |archivedate=2010-03-27 }}</ref>

The '''1905 San Diego mayoral election''' was held on April 4, 1905, to elect the [[Mayor of San Diego|mayor]] of [[San Diego]]. [[John L. Sehon]] was elected mayor with a majority of the votes.

==Candidates==

*Dan F. Jones, president of the San Diego City Council<ref>{{cite news|title=Dan F. Jones|url=http://infoweb.newsbank.com/resources/doc/nb/image/v2:136E6CB81C5E443C@EANX-1396FFA1E734090B@2416907-1396F7D9DFBED3DC@4-13986D6626BA98B8@?p=WORLDNEWS|access-date=March 19, 2017|work=The Evening Tribune|date=March 2, 1905}}</ref>
*W.J. Kirkwood<ref name="Smythe" />

==Campaign==
Incumbent Mayor [[Frank P. Frary]] declined to run for reelection. Three candidates campaigned for the open seat: Dan Jones, a [[Republican Party (US)|Republican]], [[John L. Sehon]], a [[Democratic Party (US)|Democrat]] running on the Non-Partisan ticket, and W.J. Kirkwood, a [[Socialist Party of America|Socialist]].<ref name="Smythe" />

On April 4, 1905, Sehon was elected mayor with a majority of 52.7 percent of the vote. Jones came in second with 35.9 percent of the vote. Kirkwood came in third with 11.3 percent.<ref name="results" /><ref name="Smythe" />

During the campaign, it was questioned whether a retired army officer such as Sehon was eligible for civil office. Fearing that his opponents would attempt to lock him out of office, Sehon broke into City Hall in the middle of the night of the first day of his term to forcibly take possession of the office of the mayor.<ref name="Smythe" />
